notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach target.
Idea: Process stations in position order and store passed fuel amounts in a max-heap; refuel from the largest available amount whenever remaining fuel is negative.
Technique and why it applies: Each refueling stop adds fuel from a previously passed station; choosing the largest amount minimizes the number of stops.
Invariant: max_heap contains available station fuel, and result counts refueling decisions.
Edge cases: The code appends a synthetic target station to stations, mutating the input. Stations must already be sorted by position.
Complexity: Heap processing is O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence in a strictly increasing array.
Idea: Use a map from value to index and dynamic programming on pairs of ending indices.
Technique and why it applies: If A[k]-A[j] occurs before j, the pair's sequence length extends the prior pair's length by one.
Invariant: dp[j,k] stores the best sequence length ending at values A[j] and A[k], with default length two.
Edge cases: collections is used without import. The answer is zero when no length-three sequence is found.
Complexity: The pair loops take O(n²) expected time and O(n²) DP space; the comment's O(N log M) space label is inaccurate.

Task and constraints: Find the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence by trying every first pair.
Idea: For each pair, repeatedly test whether the sum of the last two values exists in a set.
Technique and why it applies: The set provides expected constant-time membership tests while the pair advances along a Fibonacci-like chain.
Invariant: x and y are the latest two terms, and l is the current sequence length.
Edge cases: If no valid length-three sequence exists, result remains two and the method returns zero.
Complexity: The pair loops plus chain extensions take O(n² log M) or better under bounded values; set space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Simulate a robot moving on an unbounded grid with obstacles and turn commands.
Idea: Track position and direction, moving one unit at a time until a command completes or an obstacle blocks it.
Technique and why it applies: A blocked next cell stops the current movement command; after each forward command, squared distance updates the maximum.
Invariant: x and y are the current coordinates, a is direction in degrees, and out is the maximum squared distance.
Edge cases: The direction map uses degrees and modulo 360 handles repeated turns. Obstacles are stored as coordinate tuples for membership checks.
Complexity: Time is O(total requested movement steps plus obstacles) and space O(obstacles).

Task and constraints: Simulate robot commands and return the maximum squared distance from the origin.
Idea: Represent directions by four vectors, update orientation on turns, and step forward until an obstacle blocks movement.
Technique and why it applies: Each legal step updates position and maximum distance; obstacles are checked with constant-time set membership.
Invariant: i is the direction index, lookup contains obstacles, and result stores the best squared distance.
Edge cases: The implementation updates distance after each successful step; blocked moves do not change position.
Complexity: Runtime is proportional to total commanded steps plus obstacle storage, with O(obstacles) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum integer eating speed that finishes all banana piles within h hours.
Idea: Binary-search speed and use a feasibility function that sums the hours needed per pile.
Technique and why it applies: At speed x, each pile needs ceil(pile/x) hours; feasibility is monotone as speed increases.
Invariant: l and r bound the smallest feasible speed.
Edge cases: ceil is used without import in the snippet, so it requires external definition. Piles are assumed nonempty and positive.
Complexity: Each feasibility test costs O(n), giving O(n log maxPile) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Find Koko's minimum feasible eating speed using binary search.
Idea: Search between one and the largest pile, checking whether the total rounded-up hours fit H.
Technique and why it applies: The formula (pile-1)//K+1 computes ceiling division for positive pile sizes, and feasibility is monotonic.
Invariant: left and right bound the candidate speed range.
Edge cases: The method assumes a nonempty pile list and positive H as specified.
Complexity: Binary search performs O(log maxPile) checks of O(n) each, for O(n log maxPile) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether Alice wins the optimal stone game with an even number of piles.
Idea: Return True directly without examining pile values.
Technique and why it applies: The game theorem guarantees the first player can win when the number of piles is even by choosing a parity strategy.
Invariant: The function relies on the problem's structural guarantee rather than computing a game state.
Edge cases: This shortcut is correct for the standard problem's even-length positive-pile constraints; it does not generalize to arbitrary odd-length variants.
Complexity: The implementation is O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the stone-taking game.
Idea: Use interval dynamic programming to compute the score difference the current player can force.
Technique and why it applies: For each interval, choosing the left or right pile gives its value minus the opponent's best difference on the remaining interval.
Invariant: dp[j] is updated to the best score difference for the interval beginning at i and ending at j.
Edge cases: The function returns True immediately for even length or length one, relying on the standard game theorem; the DP is used only for other lengths.
Complexity: The DP uses O(n²) time and O(n) rolling space.

Task and constraints: Find the Nth positive integer divisible by A or B, modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Binary-search the first value whose count of multiples of A or B reaches N.
Technique and why it applies: Inclusion-exclusion counts multiples as floor(x/A)+floor(x/B)-floor(x/lcm(A,B)).
Invariant: l and r bracket the first value meeting the required count.
Edge cases: The upper bound 10^14 is fixed and must be large enough for constraints. The result is reduced modulo the required modulus.
Complexity: Binary search uses O(log bound) iterations and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Find the Nth magical number divisible by A or B.
Idea: Binary-search the first number whose inclusion-exclusion count of multiples reaches N.
Technique and why it applies: The count subtracts multiples of the least common multiple because they were counted twice.
Invariant: left converges to the smallest value with at least N magical numbers not exceeding it.
Edge cases: A and B are assumed positive; modulo is applied only after the search result is found.
Complexity: The search is O(log(N·max(A,B))) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Count subsets using at most n people whose total profit reaches minProfit.
Idea: Use a three-dimensional DP over people used, profit threshold, and the next crime index.
Technique and why it applies: Each crime can be skipped or included if its group size fits; profits are capped at the minimum threshold.
Invariant: arr[i][x][j] counts schemes using at most i people, reaching at least profit x, considering crimes from j onward.
Edge cases: The base state sets arr[i][0][k]=1 for every people budget; values are reduced modulo 10^9+7 only at the end.
Complexity: Time is O(n·minProfit·k) and space is O(n·minProfit·k).

Task and constraints: Count profitable schemes with at most G members and at least P profit.
Idea: Use a two-dimensional knapsack DP indexed by capped profit and used group size.
Technique and why it applies: Process crimes one by one and update both dimensions in descending order to avoid reusing a crime in the same iteration.
Invariant: dp[p][g] counts subsets with capped profit p and total group size g.
Edge cases: The import itertools is unused. Counts are accumulated and the final row for capped profit P is summed modulo the modulus.
Complexity: Time is O(k·P·G) and space is O(P·G).

Task and constraints: Return the Kth character in a decoded string without building the expanded string.
Idea: Record cumulative encoded lengths and character positions, then reduce K modulo each expansion length in reverse.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated sections map an index back into a shorter prefix using modulo, avoiding enormous decoded strings.
Invariant: acclens stores cumulative lengths and idx maps certain decoded positions to source characters.
Edge cases: The sentinel digit '1' helps flush the final segment. The function returns None if no mapping is found, though valid input should produce a character.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum boats needed to carry everyone with boat capacity limit and at most two people per boat.
Idea: Sort weights and pair the lightest person with the heaviest whenever their sum fits.
Technique and why it applies: If the lightest cannot share with the heaviest, they cannot share with anyone heavier, so the heaviest needs a separate boat.
Invariant: lo and hi delimit the remaining lightest and heaviest people; boats counts used boats.
Edge cases: The input list is sorted in place. Each loop removes the heaviest and optionally the lightest.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n) time; the greedy scan is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(1) aside from sorting.

Task and constraints: Minimize rescue boats under the two-person capacity rule.
Idea: Sort weights, always assign the heaviest remaining person a boat, and pair the lightest if their combined weight fits.
Technique and why it applies: The heaviest person cannot be paired with anyone heavier; when the lightest fits, pairing them is safe and saves a boat.
Invariant: left and right point to remaining lightest and heaviest people.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the loop is skipped. The input is mutated by sorting.
Complexity: The algorithm takes O(n log n) time for sorting and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Count original and subdivided nodes reachable within maxMoves from node zero.
Idea: Use Dijkstra to find shortest distances to original nodes and count reachable subdivisions along each edge.
Technique and why it applies: For each edge, the moves remaining from each endpoint determine how many inserted nodes are reachable; the overlap is capped by the edge's subdivision count.
Invariant: vis stores reached original nodes, while edgevis and edgeofl track edge subdivision reach from each direction.
Edge cases: The implementation uses custom accounting for partially explored edges; its edge bookkeeping should be checked carefully for revisited endpoints and overlap.
Complexity: Heap-based search is approximately O((N+E) log N) time and O(N+E) space.

Task and constraints: Count reachable nodes in a graph whose edges contain extra subdivided nodes.
Idea: Run Dijkstra from node zero, recording the remaining move budget available from each endpoint of each edge.
Technique and why it applies: Reachable original nodes are counted when finalized; each edge contributes the smaller of its subdivision count and the combined endpoint reach.
Invariant: best stores shortest distances and count[u][v] stores reachable subdivision counts from u along an edge.
Edge cases: The method assumes nonnegative edge subdivision counts and valid graph indices. Stale heap entries are skipped.
Complexity: Dijkstra costs O((N+E) log N); edge accounting is O(E), with O(N+E) space.

Task and constraints: Compute the projection area of a 3D shape made from stacked cubes.
Idea: For each grid cell, count one top-view square if nonzero and add row and column maxima for side projections.
Technique and why it applies: The top projection counts occupied cells; front and side projections are the maximum heights in each row and column.
Invariant: max_row and max_col track maxima for the current row and corresponding column.
Edge cases: The inner loop ranges over len(grid) for columns, so it assumes a square grid. The input must be nonempty.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(N²) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return words that occur exactly once across two sentences.
Idea: Combine the whitespace-separated words from both sentences and count their frequencies.
Technique and why it applies: A word is uncommon exactly when its combined frequency is one.
Invariant: x maps each word to its total occurrence count, and ans stores words meeting the condition.
Edge cases: Word matching is case-sensitive and punctuation is not removed; the method follows simple split semantics.
Complexity: Counting and scanning take O(total text length) expected time and O(U) space for U distinct words.
